source_text: Quod cum receptum est a te, apparuit nullam fuisse necessitatem naturae humanae calumniam concitandi ob hoc solum, ne baptismatis magis gratia varios habere pro aetatibus diceretur effectus. Quo persuasionis colore sublato, si quid nervorum habes, si quid ingenii, si quid virtutis, annitere probare naturale peccatum, quod vides ratione, auctoritate, aequitate destructum. Quo enim es deceptus intuitu, ut commixtionem corporum, quae Deus instituit, et conciliatricem ipsius commixtionis, voluptatem sexuum, quae tam in hominibus quam in pecoribus vigens auctorem suum eum, quem corporum indicat conditorem, diaboli opus et fruticem vocares?
pass_a_gloss: Which when it has been received from you, it appeared that there was no necessity of stirring a calumny against human nature for this alone, lest the grace of baptism be said to have more various effects according to ages. Which color of persuasion having been taken away, if you have anything of sinews, if anything of talent, if anything of virtue, strive to prove a natural sin, which you see destroyed by reason, by authority, by equity. For by what looking-on were you deceived, that you would call the mingling of bodies, which God instituted, and the conciliatrix of that mingling itself, the pleasure of the sexes, which flourishing as much in human beings as in cattle indicates as its author him whom it indicates as the founder of bodies, a work and shrub of the devil?

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS gratia=favor; Blaise grace; in iustitia definitions often 'favoritism'

pass_b_english: Once you accepted this, it became clear that there was no necessity to stir up slander against human nature merely to avoid saying that baptism’s grace has different effects according to people’s ages. With this pretext for persuasion removed, if you have any strength, intelligence, or power, struggle to prove natural sin, which you see destroyed by reason, authority, and justice. What consideration deceived you into calling the union of bodies instituted by God—and sexual pleasure, which brings about that union—the devil’s work and shrub? This pleasure flourishes in human beings and animals alike, and points as its author to the very one it indicates as the bodies’ creator.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
